categories.claim: A machine cannot originate ideas because it acts only from the arrangement of its parts, not from knowledge or reason.
categories.reason: Reason is a universal instrument while organs must be arranged for each action, so a machine can only do what its built disposition provides.

categories.claim: A calculating machine comes closer to thought than animals do, but shows no will, so it does not act from a mind of its own.
categories.reason: The test is will: the machine produces thought-like results without any sign of willing them.

categories.claim: No mind, human or mechanical, can create a genuinely new idea; it can only recombine ideas already received.
categories.reason: Ideas are given from outside (by experience or by God); understanding only compounds, divides or reassembles them, so origination in the strict sense is impossible for anyone.

categories.claim: A machine's outputs are fixed by the data and laws given to it, so it produces nothing beyond what its maker and operator supplied.
categories.reason: Calculation is determinate: results follow necessarily from given data, so the machine adds no intellect of its own.

categories.claim: The machine executes the conceptions of an intelligence but does not think; all intellectual work lies in preparing what it is fed.
categories.reason: The cards carry human conceptions into the mechanism, so interpretation and invention stay with the human who prepares the formulae.

categories.claim: The Analytical Engine cannot originate anything; it does what we know how to order it to do and only helps us use what we already know.
categories.reason: It can follow analysis but cannot anticipate new relations or truths, and claims otherwise are exaggeration.

categories.claim: Machines may in future evolve a new form of consciousness or mind beyond what humans gave them.
categories.reason: Since consciousness has already evolved through many phases, it is rash to deny that machines could develop another, independent of human design.

categories.claim: Machines are extensions of human organs that depend entirely on human direction and cannot act or produce anything of their own.
categories.reason: They obey human consciousness and only deliver reports humans decipher; when we cease, they cease.

categories.claim: New forms and ideas can arise from a process the conscious maker does not direct or know, as with unconscious cerebral action.
categories.reason: An organization can produce novel constructions outside the will and knowledge of the person who houses it, so origination need not come from the conscious author.

categories.claim: An invention yields new ideas and feelings far beyond what its inventor put into it.
categories.reason: The effect so exceeds the cause that the invention releases rather than produces its consequences, so the made thing carries humans past what they supplied.

categories.claim: An organism is not a mere machine because it produces, replaces and repairs its own parts.
categories.reason: A machine's parts exist for each other but not by means of each other; its cause lies outside it, while the organism has a self-propagating formative power within.

categories.claim: Life consists in continual self-maintenance and renewal of structure, so the organism is no machine.
categories.reason: Constant breakdown and rebuilding of substance, and death that is not mere wearing out, contradict the idea of a mechanism; self-maintenance is taken as the axiom of life.

categories.claim: The power of a part to regenerate or develop into the whole proves that no machine underlies development.
categories.reason: A complicated machine cannot be divided many times and remain the whole, so regeneration shows the autonomy of life.

categories.claim: Repair and form-building in organisms cannot be explained by known physics and chemistry, though this need not be called vitalism.
categories.reason: The production of specific form, including from a piece of the organism, lies beyond present physical explanation and perhaps beyond explanation at all.

categories.claim: Self-repair is one aspect of a single organizing synthesis that also builds and maintains the organism.
categories.reason: Generation, regeneration and healing are the same creative process; repair is described as the organism's own synthetic act, distinct to living things.

categories.claim: The organism continually renews its materials and repairs injuries so as to maintain its type, a working-order function described in physiological terms.
categories.reason: Nutritive renovation replaces waste while keeping structure constant; repair is treated as the organic apparatus keeping the animal machine running.

categories.claim: Regeneration and the organism's regulation of parts by the whole are physicochemical and need no special force.
categories.reason: Self-reproducing chemical synthesis and the flow of substances explain growth into a whole; making such matter is not beyond science.

categories.claim: Regenerative power is not a fundamental difference; machines and organisms are alike in how whole and parts depend on each other.
categories.reason: Vitalist distinctions rest on misconception; divisibility comes only from regeneration, and machines share the mutual whole-part conditioning of living things.

categories.claim: The living body is a machine, differing from human machines only in complexity.
categories.reason: Bodies are God-made or chemically driven machines; life is the most complicated form of mechanics.

categories.claim: Machines may come to repair and reproduce themselves, so self-repair does not mark a lasting line between organisms and machines.
categories.reason: Perfected machines could evolve self-supply, self-repair and reproduction; reproduction through foreign agents (as with insects and clover) still counts as a reproductive system.

categories.claim: The human body is a defective machine whose parts need outside watchfulness and repair.
categories.reason: Organs wear and fail and require careful treatment and environment, as one keeps a machine in shape.

categories.claim: Living bodies, like machines, suffer wear that cannot be repaired and ends in death.
categories.reason: Marx treats irreparable wear of instruments and bodies on the same footing.

categories.claim: An organism differs from a machine because it grows and develops by inward forces, not by a fixed model.
categories.reason: Distinction rests on growth and many-sided development rather than on repair specifically.

categories.claim: Confinement to a few simple, unchanging operations makes the worker stupid and destroys his judgment.
categories.reason: The mind is formed by daily work; with no difficulties to solve, the habit of thinking is lost, and this spreads to moral and civic judgment.

categories.claim: Narrow work gives the worker great dexterity in one task while degrading his general mind.
categories.reason: Skill and the man move in opposite directions: the hand improves as the capacity to direct the work is lost.

categories.claim: Machinery lets unskilled workers and children do work that once needed skill, so the skill required of operatives falls.
categories.reason: The mechanism carries the skill, which lowers the skill demanded and widens competition among workers; this is stated as an economic fact.

categories.claim: Replacing hand skill by self-acting machines is good: the operative becomes an overlooker whose work is easy, quickly learned, and leaves his mind free.
categories.reason: Machine-tending is lighter than the strain of hand dexterity, and moving between machines enlarges his views.

categories.claim: Machinery transfers the intellectual powers of production from the worker to capital, leaving him a mere appendage.
categories.reason: The skill and science are embodied in the machine owned by the master; the worker follows its movements and loses intellectual freedom.

categories.claim: Machine work raises intelligence for the master or manager while lowering it for the worker.
categories.reason: The division concentrates understanding of the whole in the employer or manager and strips it from the hand.

categories.claim: Demanding mechanical precision from men turns them into tools and wears away their intellect.
categories.reason: Forcing human hands to the accuracy of cogs uses all spirit on a mean act; the objection is to machine-like precision itself.

categories.claim: Machine-tending without understanding of the whole kills invention and the love of work; it can be remedied by integrating scientific education with handicraft.
categories.reason: Workers who knew machines intimately once improved them; specialization and denied education stop that.

categories.claim: Working with a machine can train a worker's ingenuity, because familiarity with the machine leads to improvements.
categories.reason: A worker attending a machine, like the valve boy, sees how to improve it.

categories.claim: Operating some machines demands intense, sustained attention and quick judgment.
categories.reason: The work is not mindless; responsibility for lives requires unbroken concentration, at a heavy cost.

categories.claim: Machines extend human faculties and require new and keener human skills to build, feed, and read them.
categories.reason: Machines are tools dependent on us; each one calls for new skill rather than replacing it.

categories.claim: Machine work changes the kind of intelligence rather than its amount: it raises some capacities and lowers others.
categories.reason: The machine's discipline trains thinking in terms of the machine process while weakening older kinds of intelligence.

categories.claim: Under scientific management workers are taught to run more advanced machines and rise to higher, more developing work.
categories.reason: Management holds the science and teaches it, so each worker climbs to more skilled machine work.

categories.claim: Repetitive machine work does not harm most workers, because most do not want to think at work.
categories.reason: Minds differ; sympathy for the repetitive worker projects the restless creative temperament onto others.

categories.claim: Machine tending destroys insight and care when the worker has no share in its ends, but understanding the whole process counteracts this.
categories.reason: The harm comes from separating means from ends, not from the machine itself.

categories.claim: Machines should take over dull, unintellectual labour, which would free people if the machines were owned in common.
categories.reason: Harm from machines comes from the property system; machines are rightly the doers of monotonous work.

categories.claim: Writing weakens memory because people trust the external marks instead of exercising their own recall.
categories.reason: Memory is a faculty kept by use; an external store lets it lapse and yields the appearance of knowledge without its possession.

categories.claim: Note-books and written aids impair memory as one case of civilized tools that replace and atrophy native human powers.
categories.reason: Every contrivance that supports a capacity from outside costs the capacity itself, as the coach costs the use of the feet.

categories.claim: Memory now resides in written aids as an external organ of the person, an extension rather than a loss.
categories.reason: Tools such as the pocket-book are extra-corporeal limbs that become part of the evolving human being.

categories.claim: Writing replaces memory, and that is a great good: it is a more extensive and faithful store than the mind.
categories.reason: Granting writing makes memory partly dispensable, the convenience and exactness of the written record outweigh the loss.

categories.claim: Written notes and abstracts strengthen memory when used as tools for review and recollection.
categories.reason: Writing heads, compends, or paragraphs gives the mind handles; those who never write need double natural retention.

categories.claim: Ideas not written down at once are lost, so a memorandum-book is a prudent supplement to fallible memory.
categories.reason: Memory lets fleeting thoughts escape; recording them is a safeguard, not a threat.

categories.claim: Transcribing and marking texts does not help memory; only attention does, and a book can be consulted anyway.
categories.reason: The hand has no closer link to memory than the eye; copying distracts and wastes time.

categories.claim: Retrieval practice, trying to recall and checking the book only on failure, fixes memory better than repeated reading.
categories.reason: Anticipation and effort engage attention; leaning on the text passively does not.

categories.claim: Writing is more precise and stable than oral memory, which changes in transmission; societies adopt it for that reason.
categories.reason: Oral tradition and witnesses' memory drift; written forms fix words, agreements, and laws.

categories.claim: Cultures without writing achieved feats of memory that literate people find almost impossible, showing what memory can do without records.
categories.reason: Oral transmission of the Veda by trained memory is exact enough to correct printed texts; reliance on easier contrivances lowers individual effort.

categories.claim: Learned people's memory for daily matters is weaker than the common man's because of distraction, not writing as such.
categories.reason: Mechanical memory works where no reasoning intrudes; scholars fail through inattention.

categories.claim: Some reading weakens memory: novel-reading fills the mind with what need not be kept.
categories.reason: Memory should hold only what serves life; idle reading exercises fancy, not memory or thought.

categories.claim: Invention imitates God's creative work and restores a dominion over nature that God gave to mankind.
categories.reason: Inventions are new creations in the image of divine works, and searching out nature is a God-sanctioned glory; the recovered power is to be governed by right reason and true religion.

categories.claim: Technical works serve God's purpose of uniting the earth and its peoples, a purpose a spiritual or poetic fulfilment will complete.
categories.reason: Linking oceans and lands by engineering is God's design from the first; the inventors' deeds are justified only when the poet reveals their spiritual meaning.

categories.claim: Industry and the planned improvement of the earth should be the practical aim of a renewed Christianity.
categories.reason: Religion prevails by giving men a physical goal: organizing scientists, artists and industrialists to improve the lot of the poorest class.

categories.claim: Machines become divine in use only when directed by a religious heart and by love rather than profit.
categories.reason: Railroads and steamboats have no sacred purpose in themselves; their cruelty comes from mercenary motives, and wielded by love they continue the material creation.

categories.claim: Human invention and progress are the work of humanity as an agent carrying out one vast design.
categories.reason: Cumulative technical progress across generations is read as continuous fulfilment of a single plan, man being the agent employed in it.

categories.claim: Invention carries an unintended higher purpose of raising the human spirit beyond its material aims.
categories.reason: The effects of invention so exceed its cause that fabrication seems to serve, involuntarily, the release of something matter holds back, though no God is named.

categories.claim: Inventive genius is a gift of Nature, not of institutions or mechanism, and the modern faith in mechanism has displaced belief in the divine.
categories.reason: Science and art arise from man's dynamical nature; worshipping Mechanism as deity is a loss of religion and a Titanic assault on heaven.

categories.claim: Technical progress is irrelevant to divine truth.
categories.reason: Revealed religion is fixed in scripture; no invention bears on any question of divinity.

categories.claim: Mechanical conveniences that claim to ease the spiritual journey are a false substitute for it.
categories.reason: The satirical railroad lets pilgrims keep their burdens and habits and bypass difficulty and humiliation, which defeats the purpose of the pilgrimage.

categories.claim: If invention destroyed labour, the Creator would have contradicted himself; the providential harmony of reason and labour shows invention is good.
categories.reason: A God who gave man faculties that destroy each other would mock him; facts show inventions increase labour, so invention fits the Creator's design.

categories.claim: Invention is a human rivalry with God, a Promethean or Faustian bid to become God, felt as blasphemy or devilry.
categories.reason: The inventor seeks to build a world himself and be God; every invention has been hailed as an insult to some god.

categories.claim: Technics is a cosmogonic act expressing man's God-given creative calling, but its creation revolts against him as man revolted against God.
categories.reason: Machines are a new order of being showing man's royal calling, yet they repeat the Fall and threaten to remake man, God's image, in the machine's image.

categories.claim: Technology fulfils humanity's wishes once ascribed to gods, making man a prosthetic god without bringing happiness.
categories.reason: Gods were ideals of culture; technology realizes them by halves, with no divine purpose involved.

categories.claim: Faith in technics is a secular religion, but invention really springs from the inventor's personal drive, not any higher purpose.
categories.reason: Rationalism made technics a materialist Trinity; in fact the inventor's passion is indifferent to consequences.

categories.claim: Religious and supernatural aspirations, not divine purpose, are what have built material civilization.
categories.reason: The longing for a deus ex machina drives building, so the religious impulse is a human cause of invention.

categories.claim: Natural law, and miracles within it, can be modelled as a programmed machine set by its designer.
categories.reason: A calculating engine set to change its law after an interval shows how apparent miracles can be part of a designed order.

categories.claim: Love for a made figure is not folly, because what is loved is the living being and beauty it presents, not its material.
categories.reason: The lover separates the form from the stone; the object of love is the figure wherever it is found, so knowing the material does not undo it.

categories.claim: Once a thing is known to be artificial, the love or delight it drew disappears.
categories.reason: The feeling rested on the belief that nature or life produced it; it is a response to an idea of life, not to appearance, so discovering the imitation destroys it.

categories.claim: Discovering that the beloved is a mechanism shatters the lover, and makes people test whether their real partners think and feel.
categories.reason: Love presupposes a mind behind words and acts; the revealed automaton drives the lover mad and leads others to demand signs of inner life.

categories.claim: Love for an artificial being is a narcissistic projection that estranges the lover from real love.
categories.reason: The automaton is a detached part of the lover's own psyche; the attachment is compulsive and self-directed, not love of another.

categories.claim: Love for an artificial woman can be knowingly chosen and is no less genuine than love for a real woman, because such passion is always love of an illusion.
categories.reason: Every passionate lover loves a personal illusion and women already make themselves artificial, so an android is an honest exchange of one chimera for another.

categories.claim: Love for a doll is a bewitchment that lasts only while the spell holds and is an object of ridicule.
categories.reason: Satire: the attachment is produced by magic and sentimental fancy; removing the charm would show the beloved as a hollow image.

categories.claim: A love for a made figure is fulfilled only when the figure becomes truly living.
categories.reason: The lover half-refuses to admit it is ivory and asks for a wife 'like' the statue; love is consummated by its transformation into a real body.

categories.claim: Artificial beings can genuinely love each other.
categories.reason: Made beings may bond through shared kind and willingness to die for one another, though their maker may fear the made partner will reject her mate.

categories.claim: A body made wholly artificial cannot love, because it has no heart.
categories.reason: Love requires a heart, which the manufactured body lacks, even when identity persists.

categories.claim: Affection can attach to a constructed person because he resembles people one loved.
categories.reason: Resemblance, not knowledge of origin, carries the attachment, though the result is a mixed and unsatisfying bond.
